title: Looking Closely
objectives: I can use ten exact verbs to tell how and why someone looks at something.
I can sort the verbs by how long, how closely, and why a person looks.
I can use the endings -ed, -ing, and -er correctly, including spelling changes.
I can write a description that shows what a character sees and does.
rationale: A shades-of-meaning ladder on looking (quick, angry, steady, careful) builds precision and prepares students for the observation language of science. The ten verbs sort into quick looks (glance, peek, scan), steady or careful looks (gaze, peer, squint, observe), and looking for a reason (glare, scout, witness). Students move from the general verb look to the exact verb that fits. Review words from earlier units (disclose, narrator, terrain) return in the discussion prompts. The passage is an invented story about two children watching birds at a pond, so the verbs appear in real events with real consequences.

words.def: To look quickly and then look away.
words.ex: She glanced at the clock and saw that class was almost over.
words.ex2: Before crossing the street, always glance both ways.
words.nonExample: Staring at a painting for ten minutes is not a glance.

apps.academic: A writer might say a character glanced at a map to show a quick check.
apps.writing: Use glance for a very short look.

cloze.s: Without stopping her work, Mia would ___ at the clock every few minutes to check the time.

cloze2.s: Drivers should ___ in the mirror before changing lanes, but never stare.

misuse.s: She glanced at the painting for two straight hours without ever looking away.
misuse.why: A glance is a very short look; two hours is not short.

visual.alt: Eyes looking quickly at a watch.

words.def: To look at someone with an angry stare.
words.ex: The referee glared at the player who broke the rule.
words.ex2: Maya glared across the table when her brother ate her last slice.
words.nonExample: A friendly smile is not a glare.

apps.academic: In stories, a character who glares often shows anger without speaking.
apps.spoken: Don't glare at me; I said I'm sorry.
apps.writing: Use glare to show anger through a look.

cloze.s: The coach began to ___ at the players who ignored the whistle.

cloze2.s: Don't ___ at me; I already said I was sorry for breaking your pencil.

misuse.s: She glared at the gift with a warm and thankful smile.
misuse.why: To glare is to look angrily; a warm, thankful smile is the opposite.

visual.alt: An angry face with narrowed eyes.

words.frame: I might glare at someone who ___.

words.def: To look steadily for a long time.
words.ex: The campers gazed at the stars until they fell asleep.
words.ex2: She gazed out the window and watched the snow fall.
words.nonExample: A quick look and turning away is not gazing.

apps.academic: A poet may describe a character who gazes at the sea to show deep thought.
apps.spoken: I could gaze at the ocean all day.
apps.writing: Use gaze for a long, calm look.

cloze.s: On the hilltop, the family would ___ at the city lights for an hour without speaking.

cloze2.s: The baby loved to ___ at the colorful mobile above her crib.

misuse.s: He gazed at the sunset for a split second and turned away.
misuse.why: To gaze is to look for a long time; a split second is not long.

visual.alt: A person looking up at a sky full of stars.

words.def: To look closely because something is hard to see.
words.ex: I had to peer through the foggy window to see the bus.
words.ex2: The detective peered into the dark cave with a flashlight.
words.nonExample: Reading a huge, bright sign from across the street does not require peering.

apps.academic: A scientist may peer through a microscope to see tiny objects.
apps.spoken: I had to peer to see the sign.
apps.writing: Use peer when someone looks hard to see something unclear.

cloze.s: I had to ___ through the foggy window to read the number on the bus.

cloze2.s: Grandpa had to ___ at the tiny print on the bottle before he could read the dose.

misuse.s: She peered at the huge, bright sign by closing her eyes completely.
misuse.why: To peer is to look closely; closing your eyes means you cannot look at all.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass in front of a foggy window.

words.def: To look with your eyes partly closed.
words.ex: The bright sun made us squint as we left the dark theater.
words.ex2: He had to squint to read the small words on the sign.
words.nonExample: Opening your eyes wide is not squinting.

apps.academic: People often squint in bright light to keep out some of the glare.
apps.spoken: I have to squint without my glasses.
apps.writing: Use squint to show bright light or poor sight.

cloze.s: On a sunny day without sunglasses, I ___ to see the far end of the field.

cloze2.s: The little boy began to ___ when the flashlight beam hit his face.

misuse.s: He squinted by opening his eyes as wide as he could.
misuse.why: To squint is to partly close your eyes; opening them wide is the opposite.

visual.alt: A face with narrowed eyes under a bright sun.

words.def: To look over something quickly to find one thing.
words.ex: Scan the list for your name before you leave.
words.ex2: The lifeguard scanned the pool for swimmers in trouble.
words.nonExample: Reading every word slowly from the first line is not scanning.

apps.academic: To find a fact in an article, scan the headings and bold words first.
apps.spoken: I'll scan the page for the answer.
apps.writing: Use scan for a quick search with your eyes.

cloze.s: Please ___ the menu and find the soup you ordered.

cloze2.s: The lifeguard would ___ the crowded pool again and again to look for trouble.

misuse.s: He scanned the page by closing the book and never looking at it.
misuse.why: To scan is to look over something; closing the book means looking at nothing.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass moving over a page.

words.def: To watch carefully in order to learn something.
words.ex: The scientists observe the plant for a week and record how much it grows.
words.ex2: We observe the clouds to see how the weather changes.
words.nonExample: Looking away while something happens is not observing.

apps.academic: Scientists observe first, and then they ask a question.
apps.spoken: Let's observe the ant for a minute.
apps.writing: Use observe for careful watching to learn something.

cloze.s: Scientists ___ how bees move from flower to flower and write down what they see.

cloze2.s: On the field trip, we will ___ the tide pools and record every animal we find.

misuse.s: He observed the experiment with his eyes closed and wrote down what he saw.
misuse.why: To observe is to watch carefully; you cannot do it with your eyes closed.

words.def: To go ahead to explore and find out what is there.
words.ex: A soldier would scout the road before the army marched.
words.ex2: We scouted the beach for shells before the tide came in.
words.nonExample: Staying home and waiting is not scouting.

apps.academic: Explorers scout the land to find safe routes.
apps.spoken: I'll scout ahead and let you know what I see.
apps.writing: Use scout for going ahead to look at a place.

cloze.s: Before the hikers set out, one of them went ahead to ___ the trail for fallen trees.

cloze2.s: The pirates sent a lookout to ___ the island before they landed.

misuse.s: The scout stayed home in bed and told everyone what was ahead on the trail.
misuse.why: To scout is to go ahead and look; staying home in bed means seeing nothing.

visual.alt: A hiking boot beside a small telescope.

words.def: To take a quick look, often at something hidden.
words.ex: She peeked through the curtains to see who was at the door.
words.ex2: Don't peek at your birthday gift before the party.
words.nonExample: Staring openly at someone in public is not peeking.

apps.academic: In stories, a character who peeks is often curious or nervous.
apps.writing: Use peek for a quick look at something partly hidden.

cloze.s: Lena could not help but ___ through the keyhole to see the surprise.

cloze2.s: The little girl would ___ out from behind her mother's coat to see the stranger.

misuse.s: He peeked openly by staring at the screen and announcing it to everyone.
misuse.why: To peek is a quick, quiet look; announcing it loudly while staring is the opposite.

visual.alt: A face peeking around a partly open door.

words.def: To see something happen with your own eyes.
words.ex: Many people witnessed the fireworks from the hilltop.
words.ex2: The campers witnessed a deer crossing the stream at sunrise.
words.nonExample: Hearing a story about an event from a friend is not witnessing it.

apps.academic: A person who witnessed an event can give a firsthand account.
apps.writing: Use witness for seeing an event yourself.

cloze.s: People who ___ an accident should tell the police what they saw.

cloze2.s: Standing by the window, we could ___ the first snowflakes of winter.

misuse.s: She witnessed the parade by sleeping through the whole street party.
misuse.why: To witness is to see an event; sleeping through it means seeing nothing.

passage.title: The Bird Walk
paras: On Saturday morning, Maya and her brother Ben walked to the pond to observe birds for a school project. Their teacher had asked each student to write down what they noticed. Maya carried a notebook, and Ben carried binoculars.
Maya scouted ahead along the muddy bank to find a quiet spot. "Stay low," she whispered. She peeked around a bush and saw a heron standing in the shallow water.

Ben tried to scan the whole pond at once, but the sun was so bright that he had to squint. He took a quick glance at the sky, then raised the binoculars and peered through them. Maya waited, and she gazed at the heron, which stood still as a statue.
Suddenly, Ben stepped on a branch with a loud crack, and the heron flew away. Maya glared at him. "You scared it," she said. Ben's face turned red.
A minute later, though, they both witnessed something special: the heron landed again, this time with a fish in its beak. Maya wrote it down. "Next time," Ben said, "I will walk more quietly."

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "squint" most nearly means
choices: close the eyes partly to see better
qs.why: The sun is bright, so Ben partly closes his eyes to see.

choices: She wants to find the heron's nest.
She wants to leave Ben behind.
She wants to find a quiet place to watch from.
qs.why: The text says she scouted to find a quiet spot.

qs.q: Why does Ben's face turn red?
choices: He is embarrassed that he scared the heron.
He is angry at his teacher.
qs.why: Maya says he scared it, so he feels embarrassed.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Maya is patient?
choices: She wrote down what she noticed.
Maya waited, and she gazed at the heron, which stood still as a statue.
qs.why: Waiting quietly and watching shows patience.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Herons are the largest birds in the pond.
Brothers should not go outside together.
Careful watching and quiet behavior help you see wildlife.
qs.why: Ben scares the heron by being loud, and then quiet watching lets them see it catch a fish.

write.prompt: Describe something interesting you saw outdoors or in a classroom. Use at least three looking verbs from this unit.
write.frame: I ___ at ___ and noticed ___. Then I ___.

study.task: Add -ed, -ing, or -er to two words from the unit. Notice any spelling change, such as dropping a final e or doubling a letter, and write one sentence for each form.

sentences: Write a sentence about someone who glanced at something. Tell what they saw.
Write a sentence that uses squint and a bright place.
Write a sentence about a scientist who will observe something. Say what.
Write a sentence about a time someone peeked and what happened.

combine.model: Ben took a quick glance at the sky.

given: She watched it for a long time.
combine.model: Maya gazed calmly at the heron for a long time.

discuss: When is it better to glance and when is it better to gaze?
How can a scientist observe without disturbing something? Use observe and one other word.
Tell about a time you witnessed something special. How did you feel?
produce.explain: Explain how the verbs glance, peer, and gaze differ. Give one example for each.

argue.prompt: Claim: Students should observe carefully before answering questions. Take a side and give two reasons.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. For example, ___.

constructed.prompt: Describe two different ways a character looks at the ocean. Use glance and gaze and tell what each look shows.
look: shows a short look and a long look
constructed.model: Leo glanced at the ocean on his way to the car, because he was in a hurry. Ana gazed at it for ten minutes, because she loved the waves.

constructed.prompt: A student needs to find a fact in a science article and watch an experiment. Explain how to use scan and observe. Use both words.
constructed.model: I would scan the article for the key word to find the fact fast. Then I would observe the experiment closely and write down what changes.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten verbs about looking, sort them by how long, how closely, and why a person looks, read a story about watching birds, practice -ed, -ing, and -er, and write descriptions with exact verbs.

notes.va.glance.v: Glance is short. Contrast with gaze on a two-ended line. Students often say look for everything; ask which verb fits the time.
notes.va.glare.v: Glare shows anger. Students may confuse it with the glare of the sun, which is a noun; tie the verb to a face.
notes.va.gaze.v: Gaze is calm and long. Ask what a character might be thinking while gazing.
notes.va.peer.v: Peer means look closely because something is hard to see. Act it out with tiny print.
notes.va.squint.v: Squint means partly closing the eyes. Link to bright light and weak sight.
notes.va.scan.v: Teach scan as quick searching for one thing. Practice with a word search and a table of contents.
notes.va.observe.v: Observe is watching carefully to learn. Students often use it only in science; connect it to reading detail.
notes.va.scout.v: Scout means go ahead to explore. Students may know the noun for a scout; keep the verb sense here.
notes.va.peek.v: Peek is a quick look at something hidden. Contrast with glance: glance is open and quick, peek is partly secret.
notes.va.witness.v: Witness means to see an event yourself. Contrast with hear about it. Discuss why a witness matters.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The sun is bright, so Ben has to squint. Squint means to partly close your eyes. I can write: When I left the dark room, I had to squint. I picture it, so I know this verb fits.'
discuss: Which looking verb tells the most about a character's feelings?
When might a narrator disclose what a character sees, and when might the narrator keep it hidden?
misconceptions: Peek and glance are the same.
Observe means look at once and move on.
extend: Write a short description of a classroom scene using five looking verbs.
Make a looking-verb ladder from quick to long and add pictures.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit glance, gaze, and observe as a ladder two days later, again at one week, and reuse disclose, narrator, and terrain when students describe what a character sees.

frames: I glanced at ___, but I gazed at ___.
wida.oral: Partner A acts out a look without a word. Partner B says the verb from this unit and a sentence that tells why the person looked that way.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (echar un vistazo, mirar con enojo, mirar fijamente, entrecerrar los ojos, mirar a escondidas) not reviewed by a native speaker; several are phrases rather than single words.
Glare, scan, and scout have other senses (bright light, a computer scan, a scout as a person); only the looking sense is taught.
The passage is invented fiction; heron behavior (standing still in shallow water, catching fish) is common knowledge.
